title: Associative and unordered containers
relevance: Staple C++ interview topic covering map vs unordered_map, complexity guarantees, operator[] pitfalls, custom keys, and when to prefer trees vs hash tables in SDE interviews and OAs.

phases.goal: Establish the two associative families, their four containers each, and how keys drive placement versus sequence containers.

must_hit.point: Associative containers arrange elements by key for fast retrieval; unlike sequence containers, the programmer does not place elements at a chosen position.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts key-based placement with vector/list positional placement and names the ordered vs unordered families.

must_hit.point: Ordered containers (set, multiset, map, multimap in <set>/<map>) are backed by a balanced BST (typically red-black), keep keys sorted via Compare defaulting to std::less, and support search/insert/erase in O(log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all four types, unique vs multi, tree backing, default comparator, and O(log n).

must_hit.point: Unordered containers (unordered_set/multiset/map/multimap in <unordered_set>/<unordered_map>) are hash tables needing Hash and KeyEqual, with average O(1) search/insert/erase and worst-case O(n) under many collisions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the four unordered types, hash+equality requirements, and average vs worst-case complexity.

must_hit.point: std::map stores std::pair<const Key, T>; the key is const because changing it would break the tree ordering invariant—erase and re-insert to change a key (or use extract in C++17).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions pair<const Key,T> and why the key cannot be mutated in place while in the container.

probes: What associative containers does the Standard Library provide, and what is the difference between the ordered and unordered families?

hints.1: Think about how elements are placed—by key versus by programmer-chosen position—and what data structures back each family.
hints.2: List the four ordered and four unordered types, then state tree vs hash table and the usual Big-O for lookup.
hints.3: Ordered: set/multiset/map/multimap on a red-black tree, O(log n), sorted by Compare; unordered_*: hash table, avg O(1)/worst O(n); map holds pair<const Key,T>.

phases.goal: Explain red-black and hash-table internals, core lookup/insert/erase APIs, ordered range queries, and iterator invalidation rules.

must_hit.point: A red-black tree is a BST with red/black node colours obeying root/leaf black, no red-red parent-child, and equal black-height on every path to a leaf—forcing height O(log n) so map/set find/insert/erase/lower_bound are O(log n) worst-case.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States BST + colour invariants and that they prove O(log n) height/operations, not merely average-case.

must_hit.point: Unordered containers hash the key to a bucket (size_t modulated by bucket_count); collisions chain in a linked list; when load_factor exceeds max_load_factor the table rehashes—one such insert is O(n) and invalidates all iterators.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes hash→bucket, chaining, load_factor/max_load_factor, rehash cost and iterator invalidation.

must_hit.point: For unique-key set/map, insert/emplace return pair<iterator,bool> (bool false if key existed); multi-variants always insert and return iterator; emplace constructs in-place; try_emplace/insert_or_assign (C++17) clarify insert-if-absent vs overwrite for map.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes unique vs multi return types and mentions emplace vs insert and C++17 map helpers.

must_hit.point: Ordered-only: lower_bound is first >= k, upper_bound first > k, equal_range is that pair—all O(log n); equal_range is the idiomatic way to visit all values for a key in multimap/multiset.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines the three range ops and ties equal_range to multi-containers.

must_hit.point: Ordered insert never invalidates iterators/references; erase invalidates only the erased element. Unordered insert invalidates all iterators iff rehash occurs, but pointers/references to elements remain valid; erase invalidates only the erased element.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts ordered vs unordered invalidation, especially rehash vs surviving references.

probes: How is std::map implemented under the hood, and why can unordered_map operations become O(n)?

hints.1: Start from the backing structure of each family—tree colours vs buckets and chains.
hints.2: For map: name red-black invariants and O(log n). For unordered_map: walk hash → bucket → chain, then load factor/rehash and adversarial collisions.
hints.3: map/set: RB-tree (root/leaves black, no red-red, equal black-height) → O(log n). unordered_*: hash to bucket, chain collisions; long chains or rehash → O(n); rehash invalidates iterators.

phases.goal: Choose ordered vs unordered based on ordering needs, complexity guarantees, key requirements, and memory/iterator behaviour.

must_hit.point: Prefer unordered_map/unordered_set for pure key-value / presence lookups when average O(1) is enough and order is unspecified; prefer ordered map/set when you need sorted iteration, predecessor/successor, or range queries via lower_bound/upper_bound, or hard O(log n) ceilings.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the default-to-unordered rule and the ordered fallbacks (sorted order, range queries, worst-case guarantees).

must_hit.point: Ordered keys need a strict weak ordering (operator< or Compare); unordered keys need Hash plus equality (operator== / KeyEqual)—and Hash must agree with equality (equal keys must hash equal).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts comparator vs hash+equality requirements and the Hash/KeyEqual consistency rule.

must_hit.point: Memory: ordered nodes typically carry higher overhead (about 3 pointers per node); unordered nodes are lighter per node but pay bucket-array overhead; unordered iteration order is unspecified and changes on rehash.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions the 3-pointers-per-node note, bucket array cost, and unspecified/changing iteration order.

probes: When would you choose std::map over std::unordered_map, and what key requirements does each impose?

hints.1: Ask what the caller needs after lookup—sorted walk, a range of keys, or just “is this key present?”.
hints.2: Tie each need to complexity: guaranteed O(log n) and lower_bound vs average O(1)/worst O(n), plus Compare vs Hash+==.
hints.3: Ordered for sorted iteration, lower/upper_bound, hard O(log n); unordered for average-O(1) dictionaries on trusted/custom hashes; Compare vs Hash+KeyEqual with equal⇒same hash.

phases.goal: Apply safe lookup patterns, custom key wiring, transparent heterogeneous lookup, and C++17 node-handle key moves.

must_hit.point: map/unordered_map operator[] silently inserts a default-constructed mapped value if the key is missing and requires DefaultConstructible T; for pure lookup use find, at (throws out_of_range), count, or C++20 contains—multimap/multiset have no operator[]/at.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the silent-insert trap, DefaultConstructible requirement, and safer APIs including that multi* lack [].

must_hit.point: Custom ordered keys: overload operator< or pass a Compare functor with strict weak ordering (equivalence is !comp(a,b)&&!comp(b,a)). Custom unordered keys: provide == and a Hash (or specialise std::hash); std::hash is not defined for std::pair so pair keys need an explicit Hash.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives both paths for ordered and unordered custom keys and notes pair has no std::hash.

must_hit.point: Transparent comparators (C++14): if Compare::is_transparent is valid (e.g. std::less<>), find/count/contains/lower_bound/upper_bound/equal_range/erase accept types comparable to Key without converting to Key—e.g. map<string,…,less<>> find(string_view) without allocating a temporary string.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions is_transparent / std::less<> and heterogeneous lookup avoiding string temporaries.

must_hit.point: C++17 node handles: extract removes a node into a node_type; you can mutate nh.key() then insert(move(nh)) or merge compatible containers to splice without copying the element—clean way to change a map key without copy-erase-reinsert.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes extract, key mutation on the handle, insert/merge splicing, and the change-key use case.

probes: How do you look up a map<string,…> with a string_view without allocating, and what goes wrong if you use operator[] for a read?

hints.1: Separate “read if present” from “insert or assign,” and think about temporary Key construction on lookup.
hints.2: operator[] inserts defaults; prefer find/at/contains. For string_view lookup, mention transparent Compare.
hints.3: Use find/at/count/contains—not []. Use map<string,T,less<>> (or custom is_transparent Compare) so heterogeneous find/contains take string_view without a temporary string.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Ordered: red-black tree, guaranteed O(log n), sorted iteration, lower_bound/upper_bound/equal_range, needs Compare/strict weak ordering, insert never invalidates iterators, higher per-node pointer overhead. Unordered: hash table with buckets+chains, average O(1) / worst O(n), unspecified iteration that changes on rehash, needs Hash+equality, insert may rehash and invalidate all iterators (references survive). Default to unordered for pure dictionary/presence lookups; use ordered for sorted traversal, range queries, or hard worst-case ceilings (or untrusted hashes without a strong custom hash).

tradeoffs.topic: operator[] vs at/find/contains for map lookup
tradeoffs.strong_answer: operator[] inserts a default-mapped value if missing and requires DefaultConstructible mapped type—unsafe for read-only checks. Prefer find (iterator or end), at (throws out_of_range), count, or C++20 contains; for insert-if-absent / overwrite semantics prefer try_emplace / insert_or_assign on map.

Raw insert/emplace on unique maps return pair<iterator,bool> and do not overwrite an existing mapped value. try_emplace inserts only if the key is missing without overwriting; insert_or_assign inserts or replaces the mapped value—clearer than operator[] when you want explicit insert-or-update behaviour.

gotchas.trap: Using map::operator[] or unordered_map::operator[] to “check” a key.
gotchas.correction: It silently inserts a default-constructed value if missing (and needs DefaultConstructible T). Use find, at, count, or C++20 contains for lookup.

gotchas.trap: Treating unordered_map as always faster / always O(1) than map.
gotchas.correction: Collisions are chained; a weak hash or adversarial keys can make a bucket O(n) (even O(n^2) over n inserts). Rehash also makes a single insert O(n). Use a strong custom hash on untrusted input or fall back to map for O(log n).

gotchas.trap: Holding unordered container iterators across insert/rehash/reserve.
gotchas.correction: A rehash invalidates all iterators (references/pointers to elements stay valid). Call reserve(expected_size) up front, or look up by key again after growth.

gotchas.trap: Inconsistent Compare (or Hash vs KeyEqual) with equality.
gotchas.correction: Ordered: keys are equivalent when !comp(a,b)&&!comp(b,a)—mismatch with == causes silent lookup bugs. Unordered: equal keys must hash equal, or elements are lost / lookups fail; weak combines like plain XOR on pair members also collide on swaps.

gotchas.trap: Trying to mutate a map key in place, or using operator[]/at on multimap.
gotchas.correction: Keys in the container are const; erase+reinsert, or C++17 extract then mutate nh.key() and insert. multimap/multiset have no operator[]/at—use equal_range.
